context:
A SaaS platform has experienced 5 production incidents in the past 6 weeks. Investigation reveals: all 5 involved the same failure pattern — a downstream service times out, the calling service retries aggressively, the retry storm cascades into adjacent services. The incidents varied in surface symptoms (different APIs affected, different error messages) but shared the same root mechanism. Current mean-time-to-detect (MTTD) is 12 minutes; mean-time-to-resolve (MTTR) is 45 minutes. The team has budget for one initiative (3 engineer-weeks):

(A) Better incident response: automated anomaly detection to cut MTTD from 12 to 2 minutes, runbook automation to cut MTTR from 45 to 15 minutes, PagerDuty integration improvements. Impact: incidents still happen but are resolved 40 minutes faster.

(B) Prevention: implement circuit breakers with exponential backoff on the 4 services that caused the incidents, add bulkhead isolation between service groups. Impact: eliminates the retry-storm cascade pattern entirely, but takes the full 3 weeks and provides no improvement for incident types with different root causes.
question: Should the team invest in better incident response (option A) or prevention via circuit breakers (option B)?
expert_answer: Prevention via circuit breakers (option B). The incidents share a single root mechanism — eliminating that mechanism is more valuable than responding to its symptoms faster.
expert_reasoning: The critical insight is that all 5 incidents share the same root mechanism (retry-storm cascade), not just the same category. When incidents are correlated through a shared cause, prevention has a multiplicative effect: fixing the one mechanism prevents all 5 (and future occurrences of the pattern). If the incidents were independent with different root causes, faster response (A) would be the right call because no single prevention investment would address them all. The team's perception of the incidents as independent (different APIs, different error messages) is a surface reading — the correlation through retry storms means prevention has far higher leverage. Circuit breakers with exponential backoff are a well-understood pattern that addresses the exact failure mode. The response option (A) optimizes the cost per incident but does not reduce incident count; the prevention option (B) reduces incident count to near-zero for this pattern. After B ships, the existing 12-minute MTTD and 45-minute MTTR are adequate for the remaining (rarer) incident types.
anti_pattern: Choosing response improvement (A) because 'incidents will always happen, so we should get better at handling them.' This treats the correlated incidents as independent events, which is a statistical reasoning error. It optimizes for the general case (any future incident) when the specific case (this particular cascade pattern) dominates the current incident load. Response improvement is the right framing when incidents have diverse causes; when they share a single mechanism, prevention is higher leverage.
